summary: Defines a mechanism by which TCP/UDP-based clients can access the OSI Directory Service without the overhead of the ISO transport and presentation protocols needed for full DAP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets a simple program look things up in a big directory without all the heavy machinery.

questions: what are the dixie operation codes
subtitle: A lightweight UDP and TCP gateway that lets small hosts query and edit the OSI X.500 Directory.

tldr.problem: The OSI Directory Access Protocol (DAP) is heavy-weight and needs a full OSI protocol stack, which small hosts such as Macintoshes and PCs cannot easily run.
tldr.mechanism: DIXIE is a simple request and reply protocol over UDP or TCP on port 96. Each packet has a sixteen octet header, and its operations closely parallel the X.500 DAP operations.
tldr.outcome: Small hosts and simple Internet applications can reach the Directory with very little coding. The memo is Informational and does not specify a standard.

today: RFC 1249 is an Informational memo from August 1991, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not specify any standard.

sections.title: Why DIXIE Exists
sections.content:
The OSI Directory Service stores information about objects, such as white pages, application and service data, in a hierarchy. The OSI protocol for reaching it is the Directory Access Protocol (DAP), an application-layer protocol that needs substantial computing power and coding effort.

DIXIE is meant for smaller hosts that lack the power or software for a full OSI stack, and for any Internet application that wants a simple interface to X.500. It follows the idea of the Directory Assistance Protocol in RFC 1202, but where that protocol exports something of a user interface, DIXIE is a more direct protocol translation. DIXIE is offered over both UDP and TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The official way to talk to the Directory needs lots of heavy machinery. DIXIE lets a small computer ask for the same things using plain, simple messages.

sections.title: Transport and Packet Header
sections.content:
DIXIE is client-server: clients send request packets and the server sends reply packets. The server listens on port 96 for both UDP packets and TCP connections. The modification operations (ADD, REMOVE, MODIFY, MODIFYRDN) must be performed over TCP, which provides some level of authentication.

Every packet is a sixteen octet header followed by data. A request header carries an opcode, a request identifier echoed in the reply, the length of the data, an options byte, a protocol version (currently 1), a search scope, a time limit in seconds and a size limit. A reply header carries a return code, the echoed identifier, the length, and the version. Unused fields are set to null octets and reserved for future expansion.

All X.500 data is represented in the QUIPU EDB format, for example the Distinguished Name c=US@o=University of Michigan.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a fixed label saying what you want, which question this is, and how long the message is. The answer comes back with the same question number so you know which is which.

sections.title: Read, Search and List
sections.content:
The read request (opcode 0x01) holds the Distinguished Name (DN) of an entry, then a null-separated list of attributes to return. If none are listed, all attributes come back. The reply is the entry, which is its DN followed by attribute values.

The search request (opcode 0x0f) sets octet 11 of the header to 0x01, 0x02 or 0x03 for a scope of base object, one level or whole subtree. Its data holds the starting DN, a dish-style filter string and an optional attribute list. The reply starts with a two octet count of matches in network byte order, then each entry preceded by a 0x03 octet.

The list request (opcode 0x10) names an entry, and the reply is a two octet count followed by the Relative Distinguished Name of each subordinate.
sections.plainLanguage: Read means 'tell me about this one thing.' Search means 'find everything that matches this description.' List means 'show me what is directly inside this folder.'

sections.title: Changing Entries and Binding
sections.content:
All four changing operations are TCP only and return no reply data; success or failure is only the return code in the header.

  • Modify (0x02): a list of changes, each as type (remove the attribute), type=value (make it the sole value), type+=value (add a value) or type-=value (remove a value).
  • Modify RDN (0x13): gives an entry a new RDN; the old value is never kept as an attribute.
  • Add (0x11): a DN and a list of type=value attributes, with multiple values separated by &.
  • Remove (0x12): removes the entry named by the DN.

Bind (0x04) corresponds to X.500 BIND with simple authentication from Recommendation X.509, and carries a DN and a password. Over UDP, the reply gives an IP address and port number to which the client should connect to get an authenticated TCP connection bound as that entity.
sections.plainLanguage: To change things in the Directory you must first show who you are, like signing in. That is why changes only work over the more careful TCP connection.

sections.title: Return Codes and Security
sections.content:
The reply header holds one of 17 return codes. 0x01 means success and 0x02 means a search found no matches. Others cover an unknown opcode (0x04), insufficient access for a modification (0x05), a malformed DN (0x06), a time or size limit reached with partial results (0x07), a modify attempted before a bind (0x08), and an unreachable DSA (0x11).

The memo's security section says security issues are not discussed. The only protections described are the TCP-only rule for modifications and the simple password bind.
sections.plainLanguage: Every answer includes a number telling you if it worked, and if not, what went wrong.
